rationale: Genesis 29:30-33 and Deuteronomy 21:15-17 share a situation and a word pair. Jacob 'loved Rachel more than Leah' (29:30), Leah is 'unloved' (29:31, 29:33), and her first son is born first (29:32). Deuteronomy 21:15 begins, 'If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other unloved, and both bear him sons, but the unloved wife has the firstborn son' (BSB). Bible Hub's interlinear shows the same Hebrew roots on both sides: the verb 'ahav (Strong's 157) at Genesis 29:30 and the participle 'ahuvah at Deuteronomy 21:15, and the passive participle senu'ah (8130) at Genesis 29:31 and 29:33 and twice in Deuteronomy 21:15; the last word of that verse is a related form (8146). In the BSB, 'unloved' occurs only in these verses and Proverbs 30:23 (script scan). Commentators draw the line from both ends: the Cambridge Bible on Genesis 29:31 cites 'Deuteronomy 21:15, "if a man have two wives, the one beloved and the other hated"', and on Deuteronomy 21:15 it compares 'Jacob, Genesis 29:16 ff.'; Keil and Delitzsch on the law write 'as was the case, for example, with Jacob.' Graded motif rather than allusion, following conn-gen9-nakedness-leviticus18, because Deuteronomy is the later text and does not name Jacob, Leah or Reuben. Graded strong rather than plausible, following conn-gen24-thigh-gen47, because the shared Hebrew is checkable and named commentators make the comparison. Whether the law was framed with Jacob's household in view is not something any source read here claims, and this row does not claim it.
